coverage.category: 26. Security, cleaning and manpower agencies, and the firms that hire their workers
coverage.found: Strong lead. Decree D/2020/216/PRG of 26 Aug 2020 and 4 arrêtés (A/2544 agent cards, A/2546 operating authorisation, A/2547 equipment and uniforms) govern private security. A 2022 decree set up the regulator ORASPC, which issues, renews and withdraws agent cards. The joint arrêté A/2025/1410/MSPC/MEF/SGG on regulation fees was under dialogue with employers (CGE-GUI) in March 2026. About 460 firms and about 30,000 agents were counted in 2020. ORASPC planned an online platform for firms to submit data (2023); whether it is operational is unconfirmed. Cleaning and manpower agencies not screened.

coverage.found: Local-content rules are scattered (mining code, petroleum code, 2019 decree). Related to K01 and K10 (quarries rejected); nothing new beyond K01.

Sanctions include closure and fines.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: Rural and semi-urban water is a delegated model: the commune owns the works, an UGSPE (user association, approved by the prefecture, bills by volume, reports monthly) operates them, and private maintenance operators approved by SNAPE are contracted by the UGSPE. SNAPE sets norms and the price (tariff cap 5,000 GNF/m3 under arrete A/2013/172/MEE of 12 Feb 2013) and must keep the national water-point file (2022 decrees). A software product, AEPConnect (TCM SARL, a Guinean start-up, with ADTTF and HAMAP-Humanitaire), already does subscribers, billing, accounting and the monthly SNAPE report, but only on 3 systems (1,139 subscribers, 8,936 invoices) per a 2026 vendor-adjacent case study. Fees at hand-pump level are collected irregularly and without clear records (Guineenews, Feb 2026). No 2024-2025 water-code reform or regulator found. Communal councils were dissolved in 2024, which weakens the commune's oversight role (PS-Eau 2024, per search summary). The 'accredited maintenance operator' and 'repair artisan' groups were not found in any register. Related: July 2025 closure of 1,724 units, many of them sachet or bottled water producers (candidate C2). Not checked: the SNAPE monthly monitoring form itself (annex 9 of the 2011 strategy, PDF not read), the number of UGSPE, and actual AEPConnect pricing or uptake.

result.competitor: No Guinea-specific ORASPC compliance tool found. In 2023 ORASPC recommended an online platform where firms would submit their data, but no working portal was found. Kolonell's blog pitches bespoke guard-management software (planning, patrol check-in, payroll) for Conakry at GNF 150-350 million, which is a vendor claim and is operations software, not compliance. A memoireonline thesis describes guard-firm management software. There are also foreign generic tools.
result.duty: Partly confirmed. Decree D/2020/216/PRG and arrêtés A/2544 (agent professional cards) and A/2546/A/2547 (operating authorisation, equipment and uniforms) govern private security in Guinea. The 2022 decree gives ORASPC the power to issue, renew and withdraw firm authorisations, manager approvals and agent cards, and to sanction offenders. Joint arrêté A/2025/1410/MSPC/MEF/SGG on fees owed to ORASPC was still being discussed with the employers' body CGE-GUI in March 2026. Not found: the fee amounts, how often fees are paid, how long authorisations and cards last, and fixed penalties. The 2023 report only mentions "dismantling" illegal or expired firms. No text of the decree or arrêtés was reached.
result.market: A 2020 government press release counted more than 460 registered firms and about 30,000 agents. A 2019 CECIDE study counted 417. ORASPC's census (reported Feb 2023) identified only 151 firms, about half the expected number. So the realistic formal buyer pool is about 150-450 firms, mostly in Conakry. No 2026 count was found.
result.reason: Regulation of the sector is real, and ORASPC has authorisation, agent-card and fee powers. But I found no evidence of how often anything has to be renewed or paid, or what it costs, and the fee arrêté was still contested in March 2026. Enforcement looks weak: half the firms skipped the census. Only about 150-450 formal firms exist, and many are informal and short of cash. ORASPC may build its own platform. Card issuance is run by the state, so software would mostly track records and deadlines. Bespoke operations software already exists from Kolonell at a high price. Low frequency, few buyers and an unclear duty make this weak for a solo founder.

A ban exists (decree Sept 2024, joint arrêté Sept 2026), but only Guinéenews reports it. The official text was not found. The duty is mostly a one-off certification and grace-period regularisation (six months). It is not a recurring filing. The only recurring item is the state's own ONCQ seizure register, which is out of scope. No operator reporting duty was found. No competitor or online portal was found, but filing is probably by hand. The market size is unknown, with no register count. Penalties are real: seizure, closure, doubled fines on repeat. The buyers are few and informal, they pay little, and the issue is a ban rather than a workflow. It is weak for a software product.

Duty texts confirmed by the Guineenews article (23 May 2026): decree D/2017/287 of 3 Nov 2017 and arrêté A/2019/3918 of 5 June 2019. They cover hydrocarbon tankers, vehicles over 25 seats, goods vehicles over 20 t and aggregate haulers. The article says the rules are not applied, apart from tanker operators. It gives no enforcement date, inspection frequency, fees, penalties or approved centres. Earlier Guineenews pieces suggest few or no working centres: the SIVITA centre has been idle for over 20 years and a new centre in Coyah only had its first stone laid in 2023. I found no competing software, but the search was shallow. No register count of affected vehicles was found. Without enforcement or centres, there is no live recurring pain, and Guinea's small buyer base is a further drag.

The instruction exists (BCRG I/DGSIF/DSIMF/012/2018, 29 June 2018) per a search summary. It reportedly requires prior authorisation, standard mandate contracts, professional cards, reporting and BCRG oversight for non-salaried agents of inclusive financial institutions. I could not read the full text because regalert.today returned HTTP 429 on two fetches. So I could not tell whether the duty falls on agents or only on the e-money issuer. I also could not tell whether aggregators file anything, or what the frequency and penalty are. No Guinea-specific agent-management software was found. Operators (Orange, MTN) most likely run the compliance and KYC back-office themselves, which leaves little for a third-party tool to do. Agents are many and poor, with low willingness to pay. Outlet counts (238k per FRED, from the claim) were not checked. Score stays at 3.

The duty looks real. Arrêté A/2023/MCIPME/CAB/SGG, per the LEAP and FAOLEX search snippets, requires a prior declaration to AGUIPEX, a DDE on the GUCEG single window, a 13 USD/t Fonds Café-Cacao-Cajou contribution paid at the BCRG, and quality, phytosanitary and origin certificates. I could not read the primary text. FAOLEX may be an older text, and the 13 USD figure is unconfirmed. The penalty is not found. The duty is per shipment and is filed on the state GUCEG platform, which Webb Fontaine runs. I found no third-party dossier software, but I ran only two searches and did not search for competitors in depth. No count of exporters turned up. Cocoa export statistics look inflated by smuggling. Few exporters, small willingness to pay, and customs brokers likely doing the filing all point to a low score.
